beats.text: Seventeen million letters, and three months.
In 1945, in Birmingham, England, warehouses held about seventeen million undelivered letters and packages for American soldiers.
The Army said it would take six months. It sent eight hundred fifty-five Black women of the Women's Army Corps.

visual.caption: Maj. Charity Adams inspects the first women to arrive, February 1945

beats.text: They worked in cold, dark buildings, three shifts a day, seven days a week. Their motto was, no mail, low morale.
When a general threatened to send a white officer to show their commander, Charity Adams, how to run things, she said, over my dead body, sir.
They cleared the backlog in three months, half the time. Then they did it again in France.

visual.caption: The 6888th on parade in Rouen, France, 1945

beats.text: In 1946 they came home. There was no parade.
In April 2025, eighty years later, the battalion received the Congressional Gold Medal.
No mail, low morale. They made sure the mail got through.
